sections.h2: Where is Hattiesburg and how does the city sit across two counties?
sections.html:
Hattiesburg is the county seat of Forrest County and the anchor of the Pine Belt in south Mississippi. Most of the city is in Forrest County, and a smaller western portion, much of it commercial land gained in a 2008 annexation, is in Lamar County.

That split matters to a seller. The tax collector, the tax assessor and the chancery clerk you deal with depend on which county your parcel is in. The 2020 census counted 48,730 residents in a city that covers 54.3 square miles, and it is the principal city of a metropolitan area that includes Covington, Forrest, Lamar and Perry counties.

Hattiesburg sits at the meeting of the Leaf and Bouie rivers, about 90 miles southeast of Jackson and 74 miles north of Biloxi. Interstate 59, U.S. 49, U.S. 98 and U.S. 11 all serve the city, and the city runs its own bus system, Hub City Transit, from an intermodal depot downtown that also handles Amtrak's Crescent.

sections.h2: How did Hattiesburg grow, and what does that mean for older houses?
sections.html:
Hattiesburg was founded in 1882 by civil engineer William H. Hardy, who named it for his wife Hattie, and it was incorporated in 1884. Railroads made it a trading center, which is where the nickname "The Hub City" comes from. The Gulf and Ship Island Railroad, finished through the city, set off a lumber boom in 1897.

The city has a historic core and a long list of older streets, and it also has land added by annexation on the west side. The city has a Historic Conservation Commission and a design guidelines manual for historic districts, so a house in one of those districts may need a Certificate of Appropriateness before exterior work. Ask the city's planning office at 601-545-4599 whether a particular address is covered.

Older homes bring familiar repair items: original wiring, galvanized or cast iron plumbing, and foundations that have settled. A buyer's lender may balk at these. An investor buying for cash usually does not.

sections.h2: What drives Hattiesburg's economy and housing demand?
sections.html:
Universities, health care, manufacturing and the military training base at Camp Shelby give Hattiesburg more than one source of demand. The University of Southern Mississippi and William Carey University both have their main campuses here, and Camp Shelby, south of the city, is the largest National Guard training base east of the Mississippi River and hosts up to 100,000 Guardsmen and Reservists a year.

Student housing and rental investment are part of this market, and some Hattiesburg sellers are landlords who are tired of managing a rental. If that is you, check the lease status and any deposits before you sell, because a written record of the lease terms helps a buyer and keeps the closing simple.

sections.h2: What is the severe weather risk for a Hattiesburg house?
sections.html:
Tornadoes are the standout hazard. Hattiesburg has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and short, mild winters, and spring thunderstorms can bring lightning, heavy rain, large hail and tornadoes.

Two recent events are on the record. An EF4 tornado on February 10, 2013 formed in Lamar County and moved east into Hattiesburg, causing EF1 to EF3 damage on the south side of the University of Southern Mississippi campus and in neighborhoods just north of downtown. On January 21, 2017, an EF3 tornado struck early in the morning, killing four and injuring 20, and about 10,000 people lost power.

For a seller, that history shows up in a few ways:

  • Buyers and insurers ask about roof age and any storm repairs.
  • Insurance claim files, contractor invoices and permits should stay with the house paperwork.
  • Damage left unrepaired is a disclosure item and affects what a traditional buyer's lender will finance.

sections.h2: What permits and code rules apply in Hattiesburg?
sections.html:
The city says a permit is generally required to build, repair or alter a residence, though some routine repairs may not need one. The Urban Development Department handles planning, zoning, permits, building inspections and code enforcement from City Hall at 200 Forrest Street. The building division number is 601-554-1003 and code enforcement is 601-554-1027.

Zoning follows the city's Land Development Code, and the building code is the 2018 International Residential Code. Permitted work must be inspected before it is covered, and the city asks for at least 24 hours of notice for an inspection.

One item deserves a seller's attention. The city's residential page notes that an owner who acts as his or her own contractor on a single-family home may be subject to the Mississippi Home Warranty Act and, if the home is later sold, may be required to warrant it for up to seven years from the sale date. If you built or added to your home yourself, talk with an attorney before you sell.

The city also publishes information on floodplain management. If your property is near the Leaf or Bouie rivers, ask about its flood designation.

sections.h2: How do Forrest County and Lamar County handle property tax at a sale?
sections.html:
Both counties collect property taxes by February 1 each year. The Forrest County Tax Collector at 601 N. Main Street in downtown Hattiesburg describes taxes as due by February 1, and Lamar County gives February 1 as the last day to pay without interest.

Forrest County explains that the tax assessor appraises property, the board of supervisors reviews the rolls after a protest period, and then the collector applies the assessment ratios and the levy set by the board and the City of Hattiesburg. The county also notes that after you buy a property it can take up to a year for the new deed to be reflected on the tax map, because the mapper works the previous year's recorded deeds.

Lamar County adds that a $3 publication fee is added on August 1 for advertising a lien. If your Hattiesburg address is on the west side, confirm which county bills you before you ask a title company to prorate taxes.

sections.h2: How can you sell a house in Hattiesburg quickly?
sections.html:
The quickest routes skip the listing process. A cash sale to an investor can close in a short time because there is no lender appraisal, and it lets you leave behind repairs, storm damage or a tenant situation that would complicate a retail sale.

Mississippi requires covered sellers to deliver a written property condition disclosure statement before title transfers under Sections 89-1-501 through 89-1-523 of the Mississippi Code, so gather what you know about roof, plumbing, wiring and past claims either way. Deeds are recorded with the chancery clerk of the county where the parcel sits.

Whatever route you choose, compare net proceeds. A listing may bring a higher number on paper, but commissions, repairs, carrying costs and months on the market all come out of it. An offer from us is not a promise of a price, and you can decline it.

faqs.a: Most of Hattiesburg is in Forrest County, which is the county seat. A western portion of the city is in Lamar County, so confirm the county for your parcel.

faqs.q: When are Forrest County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Forrest County property taxes are due by February 1 of each year. The Tax Collector's office is at 601 N. Main Street in Hattiesburg and takes payments online as well.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to repair my Hattiesburg house before selling?
faqs.a: Generally a permit is required to repair or alter an existing residence, but certain routine repairs may not need one. Call the building division at 601-554-1003 before starting work.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Hattiesburg house that was damaged by a tornado?
faqs.a: Yes. You can sell it as is, but you should disclose known damage and keep insurance and repair records. Cash buyers often take storm-damaged houses that lenders will not finance.

faqs.q: What is the Mississippi Home Warranty Act issue for owner-built homes?
faqs.a: The city says an owner who acts as his or her own contractor may be required to warrant the home for up to seven years from the sale date. Ask an attorney how that applies to your house.
